newsitem.title: USA: CME feeder cattle close strong at new highs.
newsitem.headline: CME feeder cattle close strong at new highs.

text.p: CME feeder cattle futures remained strong after posting new contract highs, with live cattle also showing strength into the close.

Feeder cattle posted new contract highs in all months with January setting a new high of 69.950 and March a new high of 69.600 cents. Feeders closed 0.850 to 0.325 cent higher with March up 0.375 at 69.350. Live cattle ended up 0.675 to 0.375 with February up 0.550 at 66.150 cents.
Feeder cattle continued to climb on demand prompted by the firm tone to the cash feeder market and expected further weakness in feed costs, traders said.

Feeder supplies are expected to remain fairly tight and tighten even further by the fall following recent very poor weather conditions in cow/calf producing areas. Good movement of feedlot cattle should also keep interest for replacement feeders strong in the near term, they said.
The latest CME feeder cattle index was up $0.05 at $68.61 per cwt, the highest price level since March 20, 1995.
E.D.& F. Man was an early buyer into buy stops, and demand was mixed on the later advance, pit sources said.
Expectations of stronger beef and live markets also prompted strength in live cattle futures, traders said.
"The likelihood that they (retailers) had a fairly good retail (beef) movement over the weekend was reflected in the futures market," one trader said.

Packers will want to continue fairly large kills if the beef market remains strong. Higher boxed beef values Monday morning should keep packer interest strong. Feedlots at the same time are holding asking prices firm after active feedlot movement last week and reduced cattle weights, traders said.
Spreaders bought February and April early after selling June against a large June/August spread by Lind Waldock, they said.

The spreading added to buying by Prudential Securities, RBH and ABN Chicago Corp to boost February which hit buy stops above 65.500 cents early. Expectations of continued large placements of cattle onto feedlots again in December, to be reported in Friday's monthly USDA Cattle-on-Feed report, had little effect on distant months, which posted new contract highs in October through February, they said.

Early analyst estimates on the report pointed to on-feed supplies at between 102 to 105 percent of a year ago. Placement estimates thus far are running 103 to 112 percent and marketing estimates at 99 to 107.1 percent of last year.
Futures closed early at noon CST in observance of the Martin Luther King Jr holiday.
